newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Argentina's Menem kicks off awaited labor reforms.
newsitem.headline: Argentina's Menem kicks off awaited labor reforms.

text.p: Argentina's President Carlos Menem has finally put words into action by decreeing three measures to kick off awaited labor market reforms.
Late Wednesday Menem decided to end long negotiations with the unions and bypass reluctant lawmakers by introducing the first laws on labor reform by decree.
"It looked like labor reform was going to just continue to be tossed around. There is now no messing around with it anymore," said an analyst at a foreign bank who asked not to be named.
Labor reforms are at the heart of the government's drive to reduce stubbornly high unemployment, currently at 17.3 percent and boost Argentine competitiveness by cutting labor costs.

Menem had threatened several times to pass the reforms by decree since the policy was first announced in August. Members of his own Peronist Party in Congress have been reluctant to pass the package and unions launched a 36-hour general strike against it and other government proposals in September.

"This is a dictatorial act by the government. Between now and the end of the year we will do something because it is not possible that things like this happen," said Hugo Moyano, head of the hard-line MTA union federation.

The measures allow workers to decide which union health scheme they sign up to and permit smaller firms to bypass national unions in collective wage talks with workers. Also, employers will now be able to appeal to the government if they want to negotiate with unions on a company-by-company and not an industry-wide basis.
Some commentators have feared the unions would derail the reforms, and the delays have increased those worries. The talks with the unions ended in a stalemate Wednesday.

This "helps cut speculation about the amount of union power," said Roberto Costa Bourdieu, an analyst at Banco Rio. "It is a good signal to the markets that the government is firm in its conviction about these kinds of reforms."
Union leaders were dismayed by Menem's decision to use decrees and Argentina's main CGT union federation said it will meet this week to discuss its reaction.
The decrees show "the president has a clear idea about it (labor reform), that he is decisive," said Agustin Etchebarne, chief economist at consultants C&E Consultores.
Even if these first measures "are not the ones that will solve unemployment, they are steps in the right direction," he said. "What is missing are reductions in employer's costs."
The foreign bank analyst said some firms have delayed hiring because they were waiting for the reforms to start.

Economists argue that the increased flexibility of labor reforms are absolutely necessary to reduce large employer costs in hiring and firing Argentine workers. Those costs are important obstacles to firms employing more workers.
